rows.subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
rows.description: A child with an external locus says the teacher gave low marks and never links results with preparation; belief that outcomes come from outside reduces effort.
A child believes practice, effort and choices shape outcomes, and tries again after losing. This helps learning, but it can turn into blaming self for things beyond their control.
A child who stumbles while reading makes a silly face and gets the class laughing with them; the joke keeps control of the moment, though constant clowning can hide worry.
A child whose mistake becomes the class joke smiles outwardly while shrinking inside. Laughing along can be a survival tactic, not a sign the joke was harmless.
A child who spelled one word wrong on a test declares the whole test a disaster and says they are stupid; anything short of perfect is filed as total failure.

rows.subtype: Approach: cold-turkey resolution announced on the first day [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student swears off all screens for a month, ignores that school groups run on messaging, breaks the rule by day four, and gives up the whole effort out of all-or-nothing thinking.
A teenager delays a project because a poor result would reveal weakness; putting it off protects the self-image but makes the eventual work worse.
After the deadline, the person calls themself lazy and vows to change, then repeats the pattern. Harsh self-talk adds the very discomfort that makes the next task feel harder to face.

rows.subtype: Feeling scared means it is dangerous [Actor]
rows.description: A child who feels nervous about a new swimming class insists the pool is dangerous; the strength of the feeling is taken as proof about the world.
Recognizing personal cognitive biases, logical fallacies, emotional reasoning, and the limits of one's knowledge.

rows.subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
rows.description: A child declares boredom after ten minutes and wants a screen; boredom is uncomfortable but can also be the doorway to imagination when adults give time and simple materials.

A parent instantly supplies a tablet whenever a child complains of boredom. The habit is kind but teaches that discomfort must be filled externally, and a short unrescued wait often yields creativity.
